Key Points 23

Question: As of September to October 2022, what was US public opinion as to whether 24

COVID-19 remained a pandemic? 25

Findings: In this demographically representative survey study of 4985 US adults, only 1 26

in 3 respondents agreed with the statement “the pandemic is over;” 43% of adults 27

disagreed. Agreement that the pandemic was over was associated with less 28

engagement in COVID-19 preventive behaviors and more political conservatism. 29

Meaning: As of September to October 2022, US public opinion was divided regarding 30

the status of COVID-19 as a pandemic and is associated with COVID-19-related 31

behaviors, underscoring important public health and policy implications of this 32

designation. 33

## 34

Abstract 35

Importance: US public health guidance has increasingly shifted responsibility for 36

actions to minimize ongoing impacts of COVID-19 onto individuals. During September 37

to October 2022, the World Health Organization continued to characterize COVID-19 as 38

a pandemic. Yet, public perceptions of the pandemic status of COVID-19 and its 39

associations with COVID-19-related behaviors were unknown. 40

Objective: To assess US public opinion on the characterization of COVID-19 as a 41

pandemic. 42

Design, Setting, and Participants: The COVID-19 Outbreak Public Evaluation (COPE) 43

Initiative internet-based surveys, administered to 4985 US adults during September to 44

October 2022. Demographic quota sampling and survey weighting were employed to 45

improve sample representativeness of the US population by age, sex, and combined 46

race and ethnicity. 47

Exposures: The COVID-19 pandemic. 48

Main Outcomes and Measures: Response to the statement, “The pandemic is over.”’ 49

Response options included Strongly agree, Somewhat agree, Neutral, Somewhat 50

disagree, and Strongly disagree. 51

Results: Overall, 5015 US adults completed The COPE Initiative surveys (response 52

rate, 56.2%), and 4985 (99.4%) provided complete information for all analyzed variables 53

and were included in this analysis. Only 1657 (33.2%) respondents agreed with the 54

statement “the pandemic is over,” while 2141 (43.0%) disagreed and the remaining 55

1187 (23.8%) were neutral about the statement. Agreement that the pandemic was over 56

was most strongly associated with having received fewer COVID-19 vaccines, lesser 57

concern about SARS-CoV-2 variant viruses, and less frequent engagement in COVID- 58

19 preventive behaviors, such as mask usage in public spaces, as well as increasingly 59

conservative political ideology, roles as unpaid caregivers of both children and adults, 60

younger age, male sex, and significant disabilities. 61

Conclusions and Relevance: As of September to October 2022, US public opinion 62

was mixed on the characterization of COVID-19 as a pandemic. Belief the pandemic 63

was over was associated with less frequent engagement in COVID-19 preventive 64

## 69

Main Text 70

Introduction 71

On March 11, 2020, the Director-General of the World Health Organization (WHO) 72

officially characterized the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) outbreak as a global 73

pandemic.1 Two days later, the President of the United States proclaimed that COVID- 74

19 constituted a national emergency.2 In the initial pandemic months, absent vaccines 75

to prevent SARS-CoV-2 transmission or COVID-19 medical treatments, community 76

COVID-19 prevention measures were implemented. Stay-at-home orders and 77

nonessential business closures were executed worldwide for the first time in a century. 78

Early support for and adherence with these nonpharmaceutical interventions3–5 waned 79

with pressures to reopen economies and resume in-person activities.6–8 80

Despite a better understanding of SARS-CoV-2 transmission dynamics, the rapid 81

development of COVID-19 vaccines, and considerable advances in COVID-19 medical 82

treatments, COVID-19 has remained a major cause of global morbidity and mortality in 83

many areas worldwide, with the US among the most adversely impacted nations. 84

Indeed, COVID-19-involved mortality and excess all-cause mortality were high in the US 85

relative to comparator countries during the initial pandemic wave through September 86

March 2022.10 The prolonged severity of the pandemic is due in part to the emergence 88

of immune-evasive coronavirus variant viruses and incomplete vaccine uptake, which 89

have thwarted achievement of sufficient population-level immunity to reduce sustained 90

transmission. The prolonged waves of coronavirus infections and associated public 91

health containment measures have induced pandemic fatigue and pandemic-related 92

political polarization, lowering adherence with nonpharmaceutical interventions such as 93

masking. Throughout the pandemic, longstanding and worsening social inequities have 94

predisposed historically marginalized and oppressed groups to both COVID-19-involved 95

and non-COVID-19-involved adverse health outcomes11,12 partly due to a higher 96

prevalence of baseline chronic medical conditions,13 more frequent exposure to 97

infections, and less access to healthcare prevention and treatment services.14 98

As of mid-September 2022, 18 months after the declaration of the pandemic by the 99

WHO, there had been approximately 6.5 million COVID-19-involved deaths and 600 100

million SARS-CoV-2 infections documented globally, with over 1 million deaths and 101

nearing 100 million infections occurring in the United States.15 The approximately 102

400,000-500,000 weekly confirmed cases documented in mid-September 2022 were 103

higher than the 200,000-250,000 weekly confirmed cases documented in mid- 104

September 2020 and lower than the 1 million weekly confirmed cases documented in 105

mid-September 2021, during the wave of the highly transmissible Delta (B.1.617.2) 106

variant.15 While comparisons are limited by the variable number and types of tests 107

performed at different stages of the pandemic (eg, approximate weekly COVID-19 108

of sustained SARS-CoV-2 transmission in the US. 112

Additionally, though prevalence estimates vary widely due to differing definitions of 113

post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection—also known as Long COVID and Post- 114

COVID Conditions—abundant emerging evidence points to long-term sequelae for a 115

substantial percentage of people following the acute phase of infection, including 116

pulmonary, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, neurologic, and mental health sequelae, as 117

well as functional mobility impairments and general and constitutional symptoms.17–19 118

Without an official announcement from the World Health Organization or US Centers 119

for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), on September 18, 2022, the President of the 120

United States twice declared “the pandemic is over” on an American television news 121

magazine broadcast. On September 20, 2022, the President addressed the 122

controversial comments at the United Nations General Assembly, clarifying he had 123

intended to convey that the US was in a different place due to vaccines and post- 124

infectious immunity. At that same Assembly, the WHO Director-General stated that the 125

pandemic was not over, and on September 22, 2022, the CDC Director neither directly 126

agreed nor disagreed with the president's assertion. 127

Public perceptions about the pandemic are consequential. A recent study found that 128

only 15% of surveyed adults living in areas with high COVID-19 transmission during 129

May through July 2022 realized that COVID-19 transmission in their local area was high 130

at that time.20 Lower perceived local community transmission levels were associated 131

with having received fewer COVID-19 vaccines, lower concern about SARS-CoV-2 132

Moreover, respondents indicated that they would change their behaviors in response to 134

levels of local COVID-19 transmission, highlighting that keeping the public fully informed 135

about the state of the pandemic, which is an essential tenant of public health,21 could 136

influence engagement in behaviors to reduce transmission of SARS-CoV-2. 137

We therefore sought to estimate the prevalence of US adults who agreed with, felt 138

neutral about, and disagreed with the statement, “the pandemic is over,” and to 139

characterize the association between agreement with the pandemic-over statement and 140

engagement in behaviors to reduce SARS-CoV-2 infections and prevent severe COVID- 141

19 illness. Additionally, we endeavored to characterize demographic associations with 142

agreement with the pandemic-over statement to identify groups to prioritize tailored 143

public health communication strategies. 144

Methods 145

Setting and Participants 146

During September 26 to October 15, 2022 (ie, approximately 1 to 3 weeks after the 147

President’s “the pandemic is over” statement), US adults aged ≥18 years completed 148

internet-based surveys through Qualtrics for The COVID-19 Outbreak Public Evaluation 149

(COPE) Initiative (www.thecopeinitiative.org). Demographic quota sampling and survey 150

weighting were employed to improve sample representativeness of the US population 151

by age, sex, and combined race and ethnicity. Respondents were not informed of 152

survey topics prior to commencement. 153

Main Outcome 155

Respondents were asked, ‘Select your response to the statement, “The pandemic is 156

over.”’ Response options included Strongly agree, Somewhat agree, Neutral, 157

Somewhat disagree, and Strongly disagree. 158

Demographic Characteristics 159

Demographic variables included in this analysis were sex at birth, age group in 160

years, race, ethnicity, highest education attainment, experience with disability, self-rated 161

health, roles as unpaid caregivers, state of residence (categorized as 4 US Census 162

Bureau-designated regions), and political ideology. Response options and analytic 163

categorizations are detailed in the Supplement. 164

Pandemic-related Characteristics 165

Pandemic-related variables included in this analysis were frequency of mask usage 166

in public and avoidance of large gatherings, COVID-19 vaccine doses received, and 167

concern about the health effects of coronavirus variants circulating at the time 168

respondents were surveyed. Response options and analytic categorizations are detailed 169

in the Supplement. 170

Statistical Analyses 171

Rounded, weighted counts and percentages were used to describe the sample 172

demographics and outcomes. Multivariable Poisson regressions with robust standard 173

errors were used to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% CIs for 174

agreement (somewhat or strongly) that the pandemic was over when surveyed, 175

Results 185

Overall, 5015 of 8930 invited eligible participants (56.2%) completed The COPE 186

Initiative surveys; 4985 of these respondents (99.4%) met secondary screening criteria 187

and were analyzed (Figure 1). Overall, 1657 (33.2%) respondents indicated that they 188

agreed with the statement “The pandemic is over” (661 [13.3%] strongly agreed; 996 189

[20.0%] somewhat agreed); 2141 (43.0%) indicated that they disagreed (954 [19.1%] 190

strongly disagreed; 1188 [23.8%] somewhat disagreed); and 1187 (23.8%) provided a 191

neutral response (Table 1). 192

Responses to the pandemic-over statement also varied by demographic 193

characteristics (Table 1). Groups in which more than 40% of respondents agreed the 194

pandemic was over included respondents who were unpaid caregivers of both children 195

and adults (376 of 609 respondents [53.6%]); those who reported their self-rated health 196

as excellent (445 of 846 respondents [52.6%]); those who identified their political 197

Discussion 247

Only 1 in 3 US adults in a large scale, demographically representative survey sample 248

agreed “the [COVID-19] pandemic is over” in September to October 2022. In contrast, 249

43% of adults disagreed that the pandemic was over, while the remaining 24% were 250

neutral about the statement. Agreement with the pandemic-over statement was most 251

strongly associated with having received fewer COVID-19 vaccines, lesser concern 252

about SARS-CoV-2 variant viruses, and less frequent engagement in COVID-19 253

preventive behaviors such as mask usage in public spaces, as well as increasingly 254

conservative political ideology, roles as unpaid caregivers of both children and adults, 255

younger age, male sex, and significant disabilities. These findings demonstrate how 256

divided public sentiments are about the state of the COVID-19 pandemic, and reveal 257

associated COVID-19-related attitudes and behaviors that could compromise mitigation 258

efforts, as well as associated demographic characteristics that could inform tailored 259

messaging strategies. 260

Inconsistent messaging about the COVID-19 outbreak has been a persistent 261

challenge over the course of the pandemic. For example, through February and March 262

2020, many US public health leaders and the WHO advised the public against use of 263

face masks to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission, even stating that they could increase 264

risk of infection, and reported  that asymptomatic transmission of SARS-CoV-2 was 265

rare.22–24 In April 2020, the CDC recommended public face mask use for the first time, a 266

social distancing recommendations for fully vaccinated individuals, citing extremely low 273

risks of infection.32 The guidance suggested low breakthrough SARS-CoV-2 infections 274

among vaccinated persons, even indicating that fully vaccinated persons need not test 275

following exposures, though breakthrough infections associated with severe COVID-19 276

illness have occurred at non-negligible rates.33 Mixed messages have continued to 277

present a challenge for public health leaders for guidance regarding the return to in- 278

person school and work, aerosolized transmission of coronaviruses, and SARS-CoV-2 279

variant viruses.34 280

Most recently, there has been controversy regarding revised CDC guidelines for 281

minimizing the impact of COVID-19, published in August 2022.35 The guidelines, which 282

do not mention the word pandemic, have been interpreted as transferring responsibility 283

to individuals to monitor the pandemic and take actions to protect themselves from 284

severe COVID-19 outcomes36 at a time when COVID-19 media coverage has 285

declined.37 Moreover, the guidelines mention but do not discuss Long COVID, which 286

can affect people across the spectrum of acute COVID-19 illness, including initially 287

asymptomatic infections,38 leading to considerable healthcare costs.39,40 Despite 288

evidence that risk of Long COVID increases with reinfections regardless of vaccination 289

The findings of the current study are also consistent with those of a study about 293

perceived local COVID-19 transmission levels,20 as both studies found that individual 294

behaviors aligned with peoples’ perceptions of important pandemic-related information. 295

People who agreed the pandemic was over and those who did not accurately perceive 296

local COVID-19 transmission levels as high had received fewer COVID-19 vaccines, 297

conveyed less concern about SARS-CoV-2 variant viruses, and reported less frequent 298

engagement in COVID-19 preventive behaviors compared with other adults. The extent 299

to which individuals are no longer seeking COVID-19-related information or the 300

information is not readily available is unclear. Given the association between these 301

beliefs and non-engagement in COVID-19-related prevention behaviors, public health 302

communication efforts to fully inform these groups are needed. 303

The findings of demographic characteristics associated with agreement with the 304

pandemic-over statement have important implications for tailored public health 305

messaging about the pandemic. Some associations with agreement, such as more 306

conservative political ideology, were anticipated given political polarization during the 307

pandemic, as more conservative ideology has consistently been associated with lower 308

levels of concern about and attention to the pandemic and less frequent engagement in 309

COVID-19 prevention efforts.42 310

However, the findings that agreement with the pandemic-over statement was 311

associated with significant disabilities and roles as unpaid caregivers of both children 312

COVID-19 outcomes, as highlighted in the CDC’s guidance published in August 2022.35 314

Indeed, COVID-19-associated hospitalization rates among disability-eligible Medicare 315

beneficiaries are approximately 50% higher than rates among age-eligible 316

beneficiaries.43 For other major risk factors, such as age and health status, responses to 317

the pandemic-over statement reflected risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes, as older 318

adults and people with fair or poor vs excellent health more commonly disagreed that 319

the pandemic was over. Perhaps not surprisingly, caregivers of children and adults, 320

who’s caregiving often puts them at higher risk of SARS-CoV-2 exposures, more 321

commonly agreed that the pandemic was over. For caregivers of children specifically, 322

perceptions could also be influenced by seasonal outbreaks of influenza and respiratory 323

syncytial virus detracting attention away from COVID-19. Further investigation into the 324

factors underlying perceptions about the pandemic within these groups is warranted. 325

Strengths of this analysis include use of a large, demographically representative 326

sample of US adults and comprehensive characterization of respondents. There are 327

limitations, including English-language-only, internet-based surveys that were 328

administered using non-probabilistic sampling methods, limiting the generalizability of 329

the findings; however, demographic quota sampling and survey weighting were applied 330

to improve demographic representativeness. Additionally, associative findings from 331

multivariable models do not reflect directionality or causality. 332

In conclusion, based on a large scale, demographically representative sample, we 333

found that as of late September to mid-October 2022, only 1 in 3 US adults agreed with 334

the statement “the pandemic is over” and that 43% of adults disagreed with that 335
